bio.en: Jessica Hische is a renowned custom typographer and lettering artist (and bestselling children's book author) whose work—logos for Mailchimp, Eventbrite, Philz Coffee, and more—has shaped how a generation thinks about brand and craft.
bio.zh: Jessica Hische 是一位知名的定制字体与字母设计艺术家（也是畅销童书作者），她的作品——为 Mailchimp、Eventbrite、Philz Coffee 等设计的标志——塑造了一代人对于品牌与工艺的认知。

summary.en: Jessica walks through the process of refreshing Lenny's own logo and brand, and explains which specific elements of a logo actually affect how people feel about a brand. She makes the case that a 'good enough' logo can serve most startups for a long time, when it makes sense to refresh your look, and shares clever productivity tips, design advice, and fun stories from the illustration world. It's a rare, accessible peek into the craft of brand and lettering from a master.
summary.zh: Jessica 完整讲述了为 Lenny 本人刷新 logo 与品牌的过程，并解释了 logo 的哪些具体元素真正影响人们对品牌的感受。她主张“够好”的 logo 往往能让大多数初创公司用很久，以及何时才值得刷新形象，并分享了聪明的效率技巧、设计建议，以及插画圈的有趣故事。这是来自一位大师、难得又通俗易懂的品牌与字体工艺一瞥。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Most people are better at understanding the feelings and sensations that typography and logos give us than they give themselves credit for, because what we are as people are endless absorbers of patterns, and information, and all this kind of stuff as we move throughout the world. We don't take time to sit and digest it, but it's still coming in and getting logged, and so even as a non-designer, I think you can look at examples of logos where something's not quite right and be like, "Something's not right here, I just don't know how to name it." But I think a good exercise is just like looking at fonts that are available in the world and asking yourself, "What feeling does this give me?"
turns.zh: 大多数人比他们自己意识到的更善于理解排版和标志带给我们的感受与情绪，因为我们身处这个世界时，无时无刻不在吸收各种模式和信息。虽然我们不会特意停下来仔细品味，但这些信息仍在不断涌入并被记录。因此，即便你不是设计师，当看到某个标志存在设计缺陷时，你也会不自觉地说：“这里似乎哪里不对，但又说不清。”但我认为一个很好的练习方式，就是观察市面上的各种字体，并自问：“这给我带来了怎样的感觉？”

turns.en: Today, my guest is Jessica Hische. In our conversation, Jessica shares the process that she went through to update my logo and brand for my newsletter and podcast. (00:01:38): What specific elements of a logo and brand impact how you feel about that brand, why a good enough logo is just buying for a long time for most startups, and when it makes sense to refresh your look, also some really clever productivity tips, design advice, and a bunch of really fun stories. turns.zh: 是的。嗯，我会主要介绍我最广为人知的领域，因为我做的事情很多，但我最专业的工作是定制排版，比如定制字体设计。这适用于各种项目。有时是为电影和电视服务。我做过电影标题和电视字幕之类的。有时是书籍封面。实际上，很多时候都是书籍封面，而我业务中很大一部分是做标志、标志更新之类的，所以基本上我就是那个什么都会的人，这样当涉及到排版时，客户就不必专门雇人了。

turns.en: I can tell you that if my team had to build integrations like this, how nice would it be to be able to take this off my roadmap and instead use something like OneSchema, and not just to build it but also to maintain it forever.
turns.zh: 我可以想象，如果我的团队需要自己开发这样的集成功能，那该有多好——能把这项任务从路线图中移除，直接使用OneSchema的服务，不仅能快速完成集成，还能持续维护。

turns.speaker: Christina Gilbert
turns.en: Absolutely, Lenny. We've heard so many horror stories of multiday outages from even just a handful of ad records. We are laser-focused on integration reliability to help teams end all of those distractions that come up with integrations. We have a built-in validation layer that stops any bad data from entering your system, and OneSchema will notify your team immediately of any data that looks incorrect.
turns.zh: 确实如此，Lenny。我们听过太多因为几条广告记录就导致多日停机的恐怖故事。我们专注于集成可靠性，帮助团队消除集成带来的各种干扰。我们内置的验证层能阻止错误数据进入系统，一旦发现数据异常，OneSchema会立即通知团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that importing incorrect data can cause all kinds of pain for your customers and quickly lose their trust. Christina, thank you for joining us. If you want to learn more, head on over to oneschema.co. That's oneschema.co. (00:05:47): Part of the reason I was excited to have you on this podcast is that I was lucky enough to get to work with you on a refresh of my logo and brand for my newsletter and my podcast, which I'm very, very excited about. It's actually going to be launching right around the time of this episode going live, so this is, in part, a celebration of the new look, and logo, and brand. I thought it'd be an awesome excuse to bring you on the podcast and give an inside glimpse into the process of updating a logo and a brand. Partly, because I think it'll just be people are like, "What the hell? How did this change? Where did this come from? Why this versus that?" and also just for people that are thinking about this for their own product or business, to understand the process and understand when it might be right for them, when it might be not right for them. Broadly, how does that sound?
turns.zh: 我知道导入错误数据可能会给客户带来诸多困扰，并迅速失去他们的信任。克里斯蒂娜，感谢你加入我们的节目。如果你想了解更多信息，请访问oneschema.co。就是oneschema.co。（00:05:47）：我很高兴邀请你参加这次播客的部分原因，是因为我有幸与你合作，为我的新闻通讯和播客重新设计了标志和品牌形象，我对此感到非常兴奋。实际上，新设计将在本期节目上线时同步发布，所以这次对话既是对新形象、新标志和新品牌的庆祝，也是为了让大家深入了解更新品牌和标志的全过程。部分原因是，我相信听众会好奇地问：“这变化也太大了吧？怎么改成这样了？灵感从何而来？为什么选择这个而不是那个？”同时，对于那些正考虑为自己的产品或业务进行品牌升级的人来说，这次对话能帮助他们理解整个过程，判断何时适合进行品牌更新，何时又不宜轻易尝试。总的来说，你觉得这个话题怎么样？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Sure. Yeah, of course. Everybody that starts a company knows that they need a logo. That is a big thing. Some people start a company and think the logo is going to drive the culture of the company, which I don't think that that is true. I think that the product itself, and the team you build, and the people you put together are the thing that should be driving things forward, but I do think the logo and the brand assets can generate a lot of both internal and external excitement and just tell people what to expect from the thing that they're about to engage with. Some people say don't judge a book by its cover. I'm the opposite, where any book... The cover of the book should be giving you incredible insight into what is on the interior of the book and setting the tone and setting the vibe so that when you open the book and read the book, it's a symbiotic thing where you're like, "Oh, I understand what I was getting into. This got me excited about starting it," and whatever. It keeps that ball rolling. (00:07:34): But with the refresh work that I do, a lot of people start companies and they have a certain amount of money. If they're bootstrapping it, they have less. If they get venture money, they have a little bit more. But what they don't want to do is spend venture money on a massive brand exploration when you're still in the hiring process, you're still trying to get early stage engineers, and all that kind of stuff, and so I am sort of a weird contrarian in this way in the brand world where brand people are like, "Brand is everything. You need to take a significant investment in brand because that guides the vision of the product or whatever." But I think being a bit more of an insider within the tech world, I understand that sometimes people start companies and have an intention to do something. (00:08:24): While they're doing that, they're building the team, they're doing cool stuff, but then the company has to pivot for one reason or another, whether a competitor immediately comes out with a thing that you're doing or the technology that you're doing gets postponed, whatever's going to feed into it, and so if you invest super heavily on the whole brand vision from the jump, sometimes it's like throwing away money if you have to pivot. What I love about the work that I do is that I understand that a lot of people have to just have something to put on decks and have something to put on a holding page or whatever, and internal teams are totally capable of doing that early work. But then if it does become successful, you don't want to get locked into whatever it is that you had to throw together before an investor meeting or something. (00:09:15): I come in then to take the existing vibe and smooth it out, address any of the concerns that came up. A lot of times, it's really utilitarian stuff like this doesn't scale well, or this thing falls apart in this context, or we never had a good avatar version of it, or whatever. Sometimes it's really specific utilitarian fixes, and sometimes it's just about growing it up and sophisticated it without losing what was there in the first place that people got excited about.
turns.zh: 好的。是的，当然了。每个创办公司的人都知道他们需要一个标志。这很重要。有些人创办公司时认为标志能推动公司文化的发展，但我认为这并非事实。我认为产品本身、你组建的团队以及招募的人才是推动公司发展的关键。不过，我确实认为标志和品牌资产能激发内外部双重热情，让人们对即将接触的产品有所期待。有人说不要以貌取人，但我恰恰相反——任何书籍的封面都应该能让你对书中内容有深刻的理解，设定基调和氛围。当你翻开书页阅读时，两者应该形成共鸣，让你感叹“原来如此！这让我对接下来的旅程充满期待”，从而让这个过程良性循环。（00:07:34）但在我做的品牌更新工作中，很多创业者手头资金有限。如果是自力更生型创业，资金就更少；如果获得风投，资金则更充裕。但他们不愿在早期阶段就花费风投资金进行大规模品牌探索——毕竟当时还在招聘团队、招募初级工程师等阶段。因此，在品牌领域，我算是个特立独行的异类。品牌从业者常说：“品牌就是一切，必须投入大量资金来引导产品愿景。”但作为科技行业的资深人士，我深知有些创业者初衷明确，创办公司时就怀揣着某种愿景。在执行过程中，他们组建团队、开展创新项目，但公司可能因竞争对手模仿产品、技术研发延期等种种原因被迫转型。若从一开始就过度投入品牌愿景，转型时可能造成资金浪费。我所热爱的品牌更新工作，是帮助客户在早期阶段搭建基础框架，满足融资路演需求。随后，我会根据现有基调进行优化，解决可能出现的实际问题——比如某些设计方案不易扩展、某些元素在特定场景下崩溃、头像设计不达标等。有时是针对性的功能优化，有时则是在不丢失初始热情的基础上进行升级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To give people maybe a couple more tactical piece of advice here, what's a sign that it's maybe time to do something with your logo and brand from you took a first pass, it's good enough, your wife made one, your husband made you a logo, it's like, "Well, this is great. Let's just go with this"? What's a sign that maybe it's time to, "Okay, we should actually at least uplevel this, not necessarily hire studio but takes something to make it better"?
turns.zh: 或许我可以再给大家提供几条策略建议。当你完成了初稿，觉得“嗯，这样也挺好的”，或者“老婆设计了一个，丈夫又给你做了个标志，然后就直接用了”——这时候该怎么判断是否该对标志和品牌进行升级了？又或者你想，“好吧，我们至少得提升一下质量，不一定要找专业公司，但总得改进一下”？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Well, one of the things is if, suddenly, you're starting to deal with the greater rollout of the look and feel of the brand. If you, at first, just basically had a really beta website and small version of the app but you're about to do a new one that kind of updates and expands it, that could be a really good time to roll it out. One of the things that a lot of people do when they're starting a company is that they'll make a logo with a font that is really popular or widely available or free. If you are about to, let's say, print a bunch of swag for new hires, or you're hosting a conference, or whatever is that event where suddenly you're going to physically invest money in making stuff with your brand on it, that might be a good time to do it. (00:11:03): One of the reasons why I tell people why having a custom logo or custom typography can really matter is that if you're using something that's available to everyone, the chances of someone else coming in and copying you are very easy and high. You might be one of these lucky companies that just out the gate is outrageously successful, but with success comes people climbing up behind you trying to copy your success. If that success is very easily copyable and people will try to trick your customers into coming their way by repeating the things that you're doing, including the branding, one way to avoid that is by doing something that's more customized when it comes to the logo and brand.
turns.zh: 首先，如果你突然要大规模推广品牌的视觉形象和核心理念。最初可能只有一个测试版的网站和小型应用程序，但现在要更新并扩展功能时，这就是个绝佳的升级时机。很多创业者刚起步时，会选用流行的、免费的字体设计标志。如果你即将为新员工印制纪念品，或是举办会议等活动，需要大量印有品牌标识的物料时，这也是个合适的改进时机。（00:11:03）我之所以强调定制标志和字体的重要性，是因为如果使用通用资源，其他公司很容易模仿你。你或许是那种一开始就大获成功的幸运公司，但成功往往会招来竞争对手试图复制你的成功模式。若品牌标识易于模仿，竞争对手会通过复制你的营销策略来吸引客户。避免这种情况的有效方法就是在标志和品牌设计上投入更多定制化元素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's actually talk about the work that you put into updating my logo and brand. From that, we can spin off into lessons and insights that you have along these lines. Overall, just high level, what's the process you go through to go through a logo refresh?
turns.zh: 现在具体聊聊你们为我的标志和品牌更新所做的工作。基于此，我们可以延伸出相关经验和见解。整体来说，请概述一下你们进行标志更新流程的关键步骤？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Sure, of course. Super high level, it's figuring out what the goals are. Some people have a goal where they want their customers to not notice it at all. They're like, "Oh, everybody loves this, but I, the person with a design eye, can see all the problems with it. I need to roll something out that fixes the problems that I see but that no one else really notices." If that's one approach to it, which is a very close in refresh where we're just trying out little things to make it feel custom or fixing things that have come up when stress-tested, whether it looks crazy when you scale it and looks like horsey and heavy-handed when you scale it too big or when you scale it too small, you lose a lot of legibility and stuff like that. That's what would be a really close in exploration. (00:12:53): For other people, they might have bigger goals where they're about to pivot the company to try to attract a different audience or things like that. They might have this really cool and successful group of people that are super users but they're trying to expand it, so then it's about, "What can we do to shift the vibe to make it include these new people without excluding our core folks?" My first round is figuring out what that scope is, how experimental, how broad are we going to go for that first round, because then everything else cascades from there. If we go really broad for the first round, then we're in this process of narrowing down the scope as we go down. Whereas if we go really close in for the first round, we're already just talking about really technical stuff. (00:13:45): This is another thing that is a little bit unique to me that not everybody else does, but I will hand off files to clients to try in situ really early on if what we're trying to do is solve utilitarian issues. Most other people are like, "No, you don't get the files until we do the final because I don't want you to run away with this or whatever." There has to be some trust with it. Yeah, figure out what we're trying to accomplish and always keep those goals in mind, and then scope out the process based on what those goals are. For each round, we're addressing different things. First round might be about just capturing the overall look and trying things as broad as we can, and then the next round is, "Okay. Well, now we have generally a look that we want, but is it the right weight? Is it the right letter height? Do we have enough details?" That kind of thing, and then we get narrower and nerdier as we go along in the process.
turns.zh:
好的，当然可以。高水平的设计在于明确目标。有些人希望客户完全注意不到设计问题，他们会说：“哦，大家都喜欢这个设计，但我这个有设计眼光的人能发现所有问题。我们需要推出的解决方案要修复我发现的问题，但用户可能根本察觉不到。” 如果这是设计思路，那就是一种非常保守的探索方式——我们只是尝试一些小改动，让设计更贴合用户需求，或者修复压力测试中暴露的问题。比如，当设计在大规模应用时看起来很糟糕，太大或太小导致可读性差等。这就是非常保守的探索阶段。

（00:12:53） 另一些人可能有更宏大的目标，比如要让公司转型以吸引新用户群体。他们可能拥有一群超级用户，这些用户对现有产品非常满意，但公司想扩展用户群。这时就需要考虑：“如何在不疏远核心用户的前提下，让新用户也融入其中？” 第一轮设计的关键是明确范围和实验程度，之后的每一步都将基于此展开。如果第一轮设计范围过广，后续阶段就需要不断收窄；反之，如果第一轮设计过于局限，后续阶段就会陷入技术细节的泥潭。

（00:13:45） 还有一点是我独有的做法：如果要解决实用性问题，我会很早就把文件交给客户让他们实测。大多数人会说：“不行，等我们确定最终方案再给文件，不然你会跑路的。” 这需要信任基础。设计师要明确目标，始终以目标为导向，调整每个阶段的范围。每轮设计都会关注不同的问题：第一轮可能只捕捉整体风格，尽可能广泛尝试；第二轮则会检查字体粗细、字母高度、细节是否到位等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. In the experience of my podcast logo, I was an ass. At the end of it, I'm like, "No, this isn't right," because we narrowed, narrowed, narrowed, and then I was like, "No, I'm not feeling it," and then we unnarrowed it and went back. [inaudible 00:15:02]
turns.zh: 太棒了。以我设计播客标志为例，我当时就是个傻瓜。最后我说：“不行，这样不对。”因为我们不断缩小范围，缩小，缩小，最后我又说：“还是不满意。”然后我们又放宽范围，重新调整。 [00:15:02不可听清]

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: That is not an uncommon experience though. This is why there's a few things that I'm not opposed to that I know people that are very opposed to. I'm not opposed to Frankensteining options together. To me, it's like I'm giving you a menu of all the things that we can do, but I'm like a chef that puts a menu together where you can combine different appetizers and different mains and they all still make sense. Some people will give you a menu and if you try to do that, it's insane and it tastes terrible. But for me, everything that we're doing, I feel like, mixes and matches fairly well, and I will let you know if it doesn't. (00:15:37): It's not unreasonable for clients to go down one path and then use that as validation or confirmation that something that we did much earlier was actually the right way. In that way, if a client ever asks me to do something, they're like, "Let's see it in purple or whatever." There's designers that will really fight you tooth and nail, because they're like, "That is wrong, that is wrong," but I know that some people just have to see it before they can let it go. Sometimes you have to walk down a path before you're able to understand what the right thing to do was all along.
turns.zh: 然而，这种情况并不少见。这就是为什么有些我并不反对的做法，却有很多人对此深恶痛绝。比如，我不反对把各种方案拼凑在一起。在我看来，这就像是给客户提供一份菜单，里面汇集了所有可行的创意方案，但我更像是一位厨师，精心设计出一份菜单，让人们可以自由搭配不同的开胃菜和主菜，同时保持整体逻辑连贯。有些人给出的菜单，哪怕你尝试拼凑，也会显得荒谬且难以下咽。但对我而言，我们所做的每一项设计都能完美融合。如果不行，我也会及时告知客户。（00:15:37）客户有时会沿着一条路径探索，然后用这个结果来验证或确认我们早期做出的决策是否正确。例如，当客户要求将某个设计改成紫色时，有些设计师会极力反对，坚称"这绝对是错误的"。但我知道，有些人必须亲眼看到实物，才能彻底释怀。有时候，你必须先踏上某条道路，才能领悟到正确的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly how it felt for me. Going back to the goals, the different goals people have when they're exploring this, you mentioned there's just little problems with the logo, it doesn't scale, it doesn't print well, that kind of thing. Another goal is people are pivoting and they want to change the vibe and the feel of the brand. What other goals might appear that you've come across why people want to do this?
turns.zh: 这正是我的真实感受。回到客户探索品牌设计时的不同目标，你提到有些人对标志存在小问题，比如无法缩放、印刷效果不佳等。而另一些客户则希望通过品牌重塑来改变整体氛围和风格。还有哪些其他目标值得关注呢？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Well, sometimes there's a legibility issue that is really glaring once you see it and then people are too close in to notice it, so this is why it's like you have to show it to a lot of people that aren't familiar with looking at those letter forms and stuff. The one that came to mind immediately when you asked was when I did a refresh for Jeni's Ice Cream, which is a really amazing ice cream brand based out of Columbus, Ohio. They had a few utilitarian things in mind. They had this long J that created this pocket of white space underneath it that made it really hard to design with, but then the biggest glaring one was that they decided to make the apostrophe of the Jeni's over the I as a cool thing. It made the word look like it said penis because of the way that J was drawn. (00:17:18): It had a little loop at the top of the J. That was the most specific fix that I've ever had to do, is make the logo not say penis anymore. But yeah, I feel like a lot of it is misreads. When you think about logos and things like that, you want it to be something that, at a super fast glance, people can read it right away. That doesn't mean that everything has to be simple, but it just means that everything has to be incredibly legible, especially when you're starting a new company or you have a less recognizable brand. Because eventually, you become a household name and then people can look at just the color and recognize that it's you or whatever, but it takes a long time building equity before you get that. Until that, it's really important that the legibility is just super tight.
turns.zh: 有时候，一些设计缺陷在你亲眼看到时才会暴露无遗，而旁观者却未必能发现。这就是为什么必须向大量不熟悉字体设计的人展示方案。比如，Jeni's Ice Cream（一家总部位于俄亥俄州哥伦布市的冰淇淋品牌）的品牌重塑项目让我印象深刻。他们最初有几个实用性需求。标志中的长J字母在下方留出白色空白区域，导致设计受限。但最严重的问题是，他们把Jeni's品牌名的撇号放在了字母I上，结果看起来像是写成了penis（阴茎）。J字母的顶部有个小环，这是我遇到过最具体的修复案例——必须让标志不再让人误解为penis。（00:17:18）设计师需要确保标志在快速浏览时易于识别。这并不意味着设计必须简单，而是要确保清晰易读，尤其是在创立新品牌或品牌知名度较低时。因为品牌最终会家喻户晓，人们可能仅凭颜色就能识别，但在积累品牌资产之前，这一点至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about actually thinking through my new logo and brand. Can you just talk about what you had in mind as you started to explore directions and we started narrowing what was the mindset, and the approach, and the vibe?
turns.zh: 接下来我们来聊聊如何真正构思我的新标识和品牌设计。能否谈谈你在开始探索各种方向时，以及我们逐步缩小范围时，当时的思考思路、设计理念和整体风格？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: I think with the Lenny's brand, you are what I would call a person that has a beloved fan base that we don't want to exclude or offend by shifting gears super crazily. When I was looking at redoing your brand, it was about what's here that we can look at that we should keep or at least explore keeping in order to make sure that it still feels the same on the other side? We didn't want to do anything super drastic. Some of the things to think about in that way are you have this sort of handwritten approach to a lot of the parts of your brand, and I was like, "How do we do something that feels handwritten, that feels like it could jive with the handwriting scripts and stuff that you were using but might feel a little bit more refined moving forward and in a way that could blend with illustration so that the illustration and the letter forms all feel like they were created by the same hand?" (00:19:17): A lot of times for me, when it comes to doing an exploration like that, it's about how do we make sure everything feels like it was created at the same time and not that we just tacked on new things? Figuring out how to blend everything together is important. Color was also a big one. I feel like people's color stories are something that is an immediate read, where if you blur your eyes and look at a brand, you can recognize it by its color, and so I think keeping your color similar was a big one too. But then I really wanted to try different approaches with the typography, doing stuff that was a little bit more clean, doing stuff that still had a bit of a funky edge to it. Because your original Lenny's podcast type had this sort of cut papery, a little bit off kilter vibe to it, and so trying to capture that but with new cleaner typography. That was really fun. (00:20:13): I was using a typeface Degular as part of it, which has a nice wonkiness to it. It was drawn by a friend of mine, James Edmondson, who I love all of his stuff. That was one of the things that we approached because I felt like it could capture the look of the original cut paperesque type. But yeah, it was really fun to try a lot of different things and work within the iconography that you had used on a few stuff with the microphones, and also marshmallows, and campfires, and all kinds of things, and just trying to make a more unified system.
turns.zh: 我觉得对于Lenny's这个品牌来说，你可以说是一个拥有忠实粉丝群体的人，我们不想因为做出太激进的改变而疏远或冒犯他们。当我着手重新设计你的品牌时，关键在于：现有的哪些元素值得保留，或者至少值得探索延续，以确保品牌在新形象下仍能保持原有的核心特质？我们不想做出过于激进的调整。比如，你的品牌设计中有很多手写风格的元素，我当时就想：“如何在新设计中保留这种手写感，让它与你之前使用的字体和插图风格相契合，同时又能显得更精致？” （00:19:17）：对我来说，进行这类探索时，关键在于如何确保所有元素在设计上保持一致性，而不是生硬地添加新元素。如何将各元素无缝融合至关重要。颜色也是个重要考量因素。我觉得人们对品牌的颜色印象非常深刻——只要你眯起眼睛看一个品牌标识，就能通过颜色识别出它。因此，保持颜色风格的连贯性也很重要。但我更想在字体设计上尝试新方向，比如更简洁的字体，同时保留一些俏皮感。毕竟你原来的Lenny's播客字体带有剪纸风格，略带不规则感，所以我们尝试用更简洁的字体来重现这种感觉。这真的很有趣。（00:20:13）：我选用了Degular字体，它有一种独特的俏皮感。这款字体由我的朋友James Edmondson设计，我很喜欢他的所有作品。我们选择这款字体，是因为它能捕捉到原有剪纸风格字体的韵味。不过尝试各种可能性也很有意思，比如与你之前用于麦克风、棉花糖、篝火等元素的图标体系相融合，努力打造一个更统一的视觉系统。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there things that didn't work as you tried to explore this process that you recall, that might be worth sharing of just like, "Oh, that was a cool concept," but didn't quite work the way you thought?
turns.zh: 在探索这个过程时，有没有哪些尝试没有成功的，但值得分享的，比如“哦，这个概念很酷”，但实际效果不如预期？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: With working on this refresh, so much of it was thinking about what are the immediate uses of the logo. Your logo, you have these very specific uses that you need it for, the avatar for the podcast being a top one. Some people, they'll design a logo and then have these illustrative versions of the logo that get rolled out for other things, but I feel like those layouts were actually more important than even just having a basic letterhead-esque logo. That's an interesting way to approach it, because usually, it's like let's start simple, and expand, and make it crazier. I felt like we had to always keep those things in play, so it was designing brand assets while also designing the logo. Sometimes you'll see examples of that in early explorations just because it makes it feel real to the client. (00:21:53): That's why there's always the tote bag. You got to put the logo on the tote bag and then it feels real or whatever. But in our case, we had really specific uses that needed to get explored very early on, and that made it a slightly different process for me. In terms of things that didn't work though, I think just trying to work on the level of detail within the illustration and type so that it could shrink down, because we knew... One of the primo examples of the logo being used was on that podcast avatar, and some of the versions felt a little bit too detailed to shrink down that much. Trying to get the balance of that, having the illustrations feel illustrative and whole, but not when they scaled up, to feel too simple like we just pulled it from a icon library. I think that was an interesting challenge.
turns.zh: 着手这次品牌更新时，我们首先思考的是标志的即时应用场景。你的标志有特定的使用场景，比如播客头像就是最重要的应用之一。有些设计师会先设计一个标志，然后再为其他用途制作插图版本，但我觉得这些布局其实比单纯的信头式标志更重要。这是一种有趣的处理方式，因为通常的做法是先从简单入手，再逐步复杂化。但我觉得我们必须始终兼顾这两方面——既要设计品牌资产，又要设计标志。有时你会在早期探索阶段看到这样的例子，只是为了让客户觉得更真实。（00:21:53）：这就是为什么总是有环保袋的存在。你得把标志印在环保袋上，然后才显得真实可信。但对我们来说，早期就需要探索那些特定的应用场景，这让我的工作流程略有不同。至于不成功的部分，我觉得就是要在插图和字体细节上下功夫，让它们能缩小尺寸，因为我们知道……最典型的标志应用场景就是播客头像，但有些版本的细节太多，缩小后效果不理想。如何平衡这一点，既要让插图保持生动完整，又不能让放大后的版本显得过于简陋，像是从图标库里直接套用的。我觉得这是一个很有趣的挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the impetuses for changing my logo, for motivating me, is my wife's a designer, as you know. She's got strong opinions about my logo, and she always was making fun of my logo saying it looked like a clip art fireplace that anyone just could just plug and play. She's always like, "Oh, that's so bad. You got to change it." That was one of the motivators. I think I might have shared that when we started working together.
turns.zh: 改变标志的动力之一，也是激励我的因素之一，就是我的妻子是设计师，你知道的。她对我的标志很有意见，总拿它开玩笑，说它看起来像一个可以直接套用的剪贴画壁炉。她总是说：“哦，太糟糕了。你得改。”这就是其中一个动力。我想我们开始合作时我可能也提过这事。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Yeah. Also too, I think that really talks to what I was saying earlier about making sure that everything feels like it was created together rather than it feeling like these disparate elements, because I think you can have an icon or logo that is quite simple as long as the rest of the brand matches that simplicity. I think, for you, the biggest thing was making the illustration and the typography just feel like it came from the same universe instead of feeling like these separate elements. When I first moved to San Francisco, I moved to San Francisco from New York, and as a New Yorker, I had an apartment with a full kitchen that never got used. I just ate at restaurants and did takeout for the seven years or whatever that I lived in New York. (00:23:51): Learning to cook, at first, when you learn how to cook, it's like you're making a pot full of ingredients and none of the ingredients are actually working together. But then the more you do it and the more you understand how these things are meant to blend and cook at different temperatures at different times, you start having this cohesive dish rather than hot ham water. You know what I mean? I feel like a lot of clients come to me and they have hot ham water when it comes to their brand. It's just about turning that into a soup, something that feels real.
turns.zh: 是的。另外，我觉得这也印证了我之前说的，要确保一切看起来是协同设计的，而不是互不相容的零散元素。因为即使标志很简单，只要品牌其他部分能与之匹配，那也是可以接受的。我觉得对你们来说，最大的挑战就是让插图和字体看起来来自同一个宇宙，而不是分离的元素。我刚搬到旧金山时，从纽约搬来的。作为纽约人，我在纽约住的七年里，厨房设备齐全却从未使用过。全是下馆子或点外卖。（00:23:51）：刚开始学做饭时，就像往锅里倒一堆食材，却完全不融合。但后来你越做越多，越明白这些食材该如何搭配，如何在不同温度、不同时间下烹饪，最终就能做出美味的菜肴了。懂我的意思吗？我觉得很多客户来找我时，他们的品牌就像是‘火腿加水’的组合。关键就是要把它变成一锅汤，让它变得真实可信。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to take a quick tangent. Most people listening to this podcast are not designers. They're product managers, founders, engineers, and folks building product. I've always wanted to see the world through the eyes of a designer, because there's so much I don't see and there's so much that affects how I think about something that I don't understand when I look at a logo, and so I thought it might be helpful just to spend a little time helping people see a designer a little bit. Let me just ask you this question. When people look at a logo or a brand, what are just elements that make it what it is, that make you feel the thing you want to feel that we may not recognize?
turns.zh: 我想稍微偏个题。听这个播客的大多数人不是设计师，他们是产品经理、创始人、工程师，或者是从事产品开发的人。我一直想从设计师的视角看世界，因为有很多东西我看不到，而这些东西又会影响我对事物的看法。比如，当我看一个标志时，很多元素决定了它的样子，让我感受到想要的感觉，但这些感觉可能是我不理解的。所以，我觉得花点时间帮助人们稍微理解设计师的视角，或许会有帮助。让我先问你们一个问题：当人们看一个标志或品牌时，哪些元素构成了它的独特之处，又是哪些元素能让你感受到想要的感觉，而这些我们可能没有意识到？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: I think most people are better at understanding the feelings and sensations that typography and logos give us than they give themselves credit for, because what we are as people are endless absorbers of patterns, and information, and all this kind of stuff as we move throughout the world. We don't take time to sit and digest it, but it's still coming in and getting logged. That's why if you see something funky in the world, you're like, "That's weird. I don't like that. I don't know why I don't like it, but I know I don't like it." I think even as a non-designer, you can see that in typography. The whole being able to recognize patterns thing, I talked about this a bit at config, it's like it's a safety thing. Looking into the world, your eyes can spot that thing that's a little bit off, and that thing that's off feels not safe to you. (00:26:08): It's thinking about when we look at a meal and there's a thing on the plate that looks like it's moldy or something like that. You understand that doesn't look right to me, this doesn't smell right to me. Your body knows it before your brain knows it. Even as a non-designer, I think you can look at examples of logos where something's not quite right and be like, "Something's not right here, I just don't know how to name it." But I think a good exercise is just looking at fonts that are available in the world and asking yourself, "What feeling does this give me?" and just write them down. It doesn't matter, just give yourself permission to say whatever is happening in your mind, the first thing. Don't overanalyze it. Just look at it and be like, "That feels calm to me. That feels exciting to me. That feels whatever to me." (00:27:00): The more you do that, the more you can start seeing similarities in the ones that feel exciting, and the ones that feel calm, and the ones that feel whatever, and then get into analyze mode of, "Oh, these 10 things that I said feel calm are a lighter weight, have more generous spacing, have rounded edges, have rounder bowls to the letter forms." You just start seeing commonalities between the things. It's just about seeing them all together to understand what those similarities are. I think anybody can do that. I mean, you're not going to have the language of the leg of the R and the tittle of the I. Don't worry about that. You don't have to know typography language to think about it, but anybody's capable of doing that. It can be really fun to just stop and ask yourself and notice.
turns.zh: 我认为大多数人比他们自己想象的更善于理解字体和标志给我们带来的感觉和情绪，因为我们作为人类，无时无刻不在吸收各种模式和信息。当我们在世界上行走时，虽然没有时间停下来仔细消化这些信息，但它们一直在进入我们的视野并被记录下来。这就是为什么当你在现实中看到一些奇怪的东西时，你会说：“这太奇怪了。我不喜欢它。我不知道为什么不喜欢，但就是不喜欢。” 即使你不是设计师，你也能从字体中看到这一点。能够识别模式的能力，我在 Config 大会上稍微提过一点，这就像是一种安全机制。观察世界时，你的眼睛能发现一些微妙的异常，而这种异常会让你觉得不安全。（00:26:08）：这就像我们看一顿饭时，盘子里有看起来发霉的东西。你会意识到这不对劲，闻起来也不对劲。你的身体比大脑更先察觉到问题。即使你不是设计师，我认为你也能看一些标志设计不尽如人意的例子，并说：“这里有问题，虽然我不知道怎么形容。” 但我觉得一个很好的练习就是看看世界上现有的字体，然后问自己：“这给我什么感觉？”只需允许自己说出脑海中最初浮现的想法，不用过度分析。只需观察，然后说：“这让我感到平静。这让我感到兴奋。这让我觉得无所谓。” （00:27:00）：你越这样做，就越能开始发现那些让人兴奋、平静或无所谓的感觉之间的相似之处，然后再进入分析模式，比如：“哦，我说感觉平静的这10个字体，字重更轻，间距更宽，边缘更圆，字母形状更圆润。” 你就会开始发现它们之间的共性。任何人都能做到这一点。我的意思是，你不必掌握R的横折和I的点饰的专业术语。不用担心这些。你不需要懂排版术语就能思考这些问题，但任何人都能做到。停下来问问自己，留意一下这些细节真的很有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is great. I want to go actually a little deeper. What I'm hearing is look at something, tap into the feeling you feel when you look at it, actually pay attention to it because there's wisdom in that. The specific things that you pointed out that impact that feeling are, you mentioned, spacing between the letters, the edges. I imagine there's just the color of it. What other specific elements impact the way someone feels when they look at a logo?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我还想更深入探讨一下。我听到的核心观点是，观察某个事物时，要留意自己看到它时的感受，因为这其中蕴含着智慧。具体来说，影响这种感受的因素包括字母间距、边缘设计等。我想还有颜色因素。还有哪些具体元素会影响人们看待标志时的感受呢？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: There's the width of the letter, so if it's really narrow versus really wide. I always think about the width, the weight, [inaudible 00:28:35] facing, sort of detailed treatment of things, whether things are very hard and jagged or soft and how soft it is. Sometimes we just add a tiny bit of softness so that it just feels printed. You can take a typeface like Helvetica, just the one everybody knows. But if you take Helvetica and just ever so slightly round the edges just a little bit, all of a sudden, you have this typeface that feels more vintage, or softer, or whatever, because we're perceiving it, we would perceive it if it were printed on paper versus perceiving it as this hard geometric piece of technology that we're viewing. You know what I mean? (00:29:20): I know that it's because when you look at stuff printed on a page, it bleeds into the paper a little bit, which means that that softness reminds us in our bodies of a thing that we've seen that was printed. It's cool to sort of walk back your feelings also. You'll look at something and go, "That feels like this," and then ask yourself why does it feel like that. It might be because you saw it on a flyer for a band when you were 22, and it brought out that feeling in you of what it felt like to be 22 at that thing. That's a very specific feeling to you, but it can inform your decisions about design, because you can be like, "Oh, I'm not that much of a special snowflake." Other people might have that same reaction but have different experiences that are adjacent to that reaction. (00:30:08): It's cool because you are reverse-justifying decisions. I think that's a really fun exercise to do, is to Song Exploder your intuition. You make a decision intuitively or look at something and intuit what you feel from it, and then really try to dive in, "Why do I feel that way? What could this have reminded me of that made me feel that way?" You have to be just so forgiving and loose with yourself as you do it because then you'll get into some really weird stuff, and that's really great inspiration juice for picking other things.
turns.zh: 字母的宽度也很重要，比如字母过窄或过宽。我总会考虑字体宽度、粗细，以及细节处理——比如字体是否棱角分明或柔和顺滑。有些时候，我们会添加一点柔和感，让设计更具印刷感，比如大家熟知的Helvetica字体。只需将Helvetica的边缘稍稍圆润，瞬间就能营造出复古或柔和的质感，因为我们会把它与印刷品联系起来，而非冷冰冰的数字设备屏幕。懂我的意思吧？（00:29:20）比如印刷品会与纸张有轻微的融合，这种柔和感会让我们联想到曾经见过的印刷品。这种反向追溯情绪的做法很酷。当你看到某物时，会说“这让我想起某种感觉”，然后追问原因。或许是因为你22岁时看到某个乐队传单，勾起那种青春岁月的记忆。这对你设计决策很有启发——你会意识到自己并非独一无二。其他人可能也有类似反应，但因经历不同而有所不同。（00:30:08）这种逆向验证决策的过程很有趣。比如剖析自己的直觉。直觉下决定后，再仔细剖析背后的原因：“为什么我会有这种感觉？它让我想起了什么？” 在这个过程中，要保持开放的心态，避免钻牛角尖，这样才能获得灵感，用于其他设计决策。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the exercise that you gave. The one you gave earlier is look at a bunch of fonts, look at your font folder. Is that a place to go, just open up your font folder and just go through them?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢你提到的练习。之前你提到要浏览字体库，打开字体文件夹看看。这样做有意义吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Totally. Look at your font folder, or go to MyFonts, or a place where there's a ton of fonts, and just search for something. Search for sans serif or whatever. Search for a really basic category of fonts. Serif, sans serif, script, whatever, the top level edge of stuff, and then just page through, page through, page through. Screenshot stuff that you like and make a folder full of screenshots, and then you can take those screenshots and start categorizing them. "Oh, this one feels feminine. This one feels masculine, this one feels aggressive. This one feels whatever." Just take some notes on it. Then, you ask yourself, "Well, why did I feel that way?" You're like, "Oh, well, this feels feminine because it reminds me of wedding invitations," and wedding invitations feel inherently bridey versus groomy. All of a sudden, you're like, "Okay. Well, now I know that if I'm going to use a script for something, this zone of script feels very wedding, so maybe I avoid that for this brand that's actually a cutting edge food packaging company or whatever because it feels too aligned with that industry." (00:32:10): Stereotypes are real and trends are real, and what can sometimes happen is some industry usurps an entire style for a period of time. If you use anything within that style, it's like you're aligning yourself to that industry. I mean, everybody that does branding, one of the things that they do is they analyze the competitors of the company. You just look at a landscape of what are all the competitors doing, what is their visual vibe, and do I lean into that or do I avoid that? If I lean into it, then I'm immediately getting this... Everyone that looks at it understands I'm a FinTech company because I look like a FinTech company. If my whole thing is I'm trying to be divergent from that, I'm trying to show how different I am from the status quo, then you use it as a reactionary thing of I want to do nothing like that and do something really different so people understand this isn't just another FinTech company.
turns.zh:
完全没错。看看你的字体文件夹，或者去MyFonts之类的字体资源网站，搜索一些字体。比如无衬线字体之类的，或者最基础的字体类别——衬线字体、无衬线字体、手写字体等等。先浏览一遍，挑选喜欢的字体截图，整理成一个文件夹。然后你可以逐一分析这些字体：“嗯，这个字体感觉很女性化。这个字体感觉很男性化。这个字体感觉很强势。”记下你的观察结果。接着问自己：“为什么会有这种感觉？”比如，“哦，嗯，这个字体让我联想到婚礼请柬，所以感觉比较女性化，而婚礼请柬通常偏向新娘风格。”突然你意识到：“好吧，那如果我要为一个前沿的食品包装公司设计品牌，可能就不能用这种带有婚礼元素的字体了，因为这会让品牌过于贴合传统行业的固有印象。”  

（00:32:10）刻板印象是真实存在的，潮流趋势也是如此。有时某个行业会暂时主导某种风格。若你使用了该风格的元素，就等于在向该行业靠拢。比如品牌设计师通常会分析竞争对手的视觉风格：观察行业同行如何定位品牌形象，然后决定是顺势而为还是另辟蹊径。若想突显品牌的独特性，可能需要反其道而行之，让人们一目了然你的品牌与传统FinTech公司的不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I'm thinking green. The color green has to be a part of the logo if you want to be a FinTech company.
turns.zh: 对啊。我在考虑用绿色。如果想打造FinTech品牌，绿色肯定是标识的一部分。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. If you're trying to be weird, then you're like teal.
turns.zh: 没错。如果想标新立异，就选蓝绿色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On this topic of seeing a designer, is there any other tip, just before we move on to a different topic, of just how someone could learn to see a designer a little bit more?
turns.zh: 关于找设计师这件事，在转到下一个话题前，还有什么建议能帮助人们更好地理解设计师的思维方式吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Yeah. Another thing to notice, because I'm assuming you're... Product people, I feel like a lot of product people end up having some engineering background, whether or not they're engineers themselves. They have to interface with the engineers and they build stuff, and so they come at it from a data standpoint. I can always tell when there's an engineer that has suddenly got taken an interest in type design and is now a type designer, because everything is very, very regular. You can draw a grid on top of everything and the lines all line up perfectly. You see lots of reverse justification of that when people are making logos and they have a more engineering background. The thing to notice, that is interesting within type, is that, yes, you're absolutely following rules, but you're breaking those rules quite often to correct for optical tricks. (00:34:24): If you look at a geometric sans serif, for instance, that's like a category of sans serifs, and they're meant to have a lot of really strong geometry, be very regular, like most of the sans that you think of that you're like, "I'm in love with this over the last 10 years," like geometric sanses. But when you really start to examine them, you notice that there's all these little things that people are doing to make them look perfectly geometric even though they are not mathematically perfectly geometric. That's another thing that you can do, whether you're doing it in Figma or doing it somewhere else, is just type out a couple of lowercase letters. Lowercase specifically are really good for analyzing this because they're smaller than the uppercase letters. You usually have to accommodate for the weight a little bit differently. You'll notice that when strokes combine, so say I have an A and I'm combining the lower bowl of the A, I'm going to get a little thinner as I come into that. (00:35:23): Or say I have a two-storey A, so a two-storey A is the one that's like this and then a bowl, you might notice that this vertical of the A there, the bowl actually eats into that stroke a little bit to erase a little bit of that added weight that would've been perceived optically had you kept everything perfectly regular. It's weird because you end up creating something that's perfect and then have to make it not perfect in order to make it be perceived as perfect. That's another just fun thing to start noticing. You notice it a lot more on typefaces and typography that is heavier in weight, because when things are heavier weight, you're constantly managing these really inky moments where things join together and you have to subtract a bunch of weight from that so that it doesn't get perceived as this dark mark where the letter is happening. (00:36:22): I think about lowercase Rs and lowercase Ns, where the shoulder of the N or the R comes out, sometimes the top of the R is actually narrower at the top than it is on the bottom, and that's to try to subtract some of that weight in there where that join happens. Anyway, that's just a fun thing to notice that you have to do that. Once you start seeing it, you start seeing where it happens more often, and the answer of why it happens is because correcting for this optical weight issue. You're like, "Oh, man. Now I have x-ray vision. I can see all these weird things I've never seen before." It's very fun. But anyway, a lot of people, when they first start out doing typography, whether you're an engineer or whether you are a designer, they don't account for that. I can always just look at something and see whether someone is truly an expert at typography or whether this is a fun hobby for them when they're pretty fresh at it.
turns.zh:
是啊。这里还有一点值得注意——因为我猜你们都是产品人员——我觉得很多产品从业者最终都会有一些工程背景，无论他们自己是否是工程师。他们需要与工程师打交道、开发产品，所以他们会从数据的角度去思考问题。我总能辨别出那些突然对字体设计感兴趣、自诩为字体设计师的工程师，因为他们的作品都极其规整。只要在作品上画个网格，线条就能完美对齐。这种反向校正在标志设计中尤为常见，尤其是那些有工程背景的人设计的标志。  

在字体设计中，有趣的一点在于，你确实在遵循规则，但又经常为了纠正视觉错觉而打破这些规则。（00:34:24）比如几何无衬线字体，这类字体本应具有极强的几何感和规整性，就像我们过去十年里痴迷的几何无衬线字体。但仔细观察会发现，有些细节被刻意调整以营造完美几何感，即便在数学上并非完美。  

无论是在Figma还是其他平台，你都可以先写几个小写字母。小写字母更适合分析，因为它们比大写字母更细。通常需要针对笔画粗细进行微调。比如，当A的下部与另一个字母结合时，笔画会变细。（00:35:23）或者是两层结构的A字母（上部是A，下部是碗状），会发现A的垂线会稍微侵入下部笔画，以消除因保持笔画规则而产生的视觉厚重感。  

这很奇妙——你创造出完美的作品，却又不得不让它显得不完美，才能让观者感知到它的完美。这种趣味在字体和排版中最明显，因为厚重字体需要不断处理墨水感强的连接处，需要主动削减笔画以避免视觉上的厚重感。  

比如小写R和N，N或R的肩部有时会延伸，R的顶部甚至比底部更窄，这都是为了削减连接处的笔画重量。总之，这些细节值得留意，学会主动发现它们的存在。  

一旦你开始留意，就会发现这种现象更为普遍，而背后的原因在于校正视觉重量问题。你会感叹：“天哪，我现在有透视眼了，能看到以前从未注意的奇怪之处。”这真是乐趣无穷。不过许多初涉排版的人，无论是工程师还是设计师，都忽视了这些细节。我总能一眼看出某人是否是真正的高手。
排版设计是否是一种专业技能，还是说对于刚入门的新手而言，这只不过是一种充满乐趣的业余爱好？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The exercise here is open up Figma, start typing, and make it really big so you can basically see the font really zoomed in.
turns.zh: 接下来的练习是打开Figma，开始输入文字，然后把字体放大到最大，这样你就能清晰地看到放大后的字体效果了。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: A single letter.
turns.zh: 一个字母。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A single letter.
turns.zh: 一个字母。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Make a single letter the whole page and then just draw some vertical lines, or do the thing where you draw a little circle or whatever and see if that circle is the same size at the point where two strokes join together or the point where the stroke is just vertical and on its own. You'll notice that there's differences even in typography that's meant to look extremely rigid and geometric.
turns.zh: 把整个页面都做成一个字母，然后画一些垂直线，或者画一个小圆圈之类的，看看这个圆圈在两条笔画连接的地方，或者在笔画垂直独立的地方，是否大小一致。你会发现，即使是那些看起来极其规整、几何化的字体设计，也存在细微的差别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to my logo just to close the loop there. Talk about just the final result that we landed on, and why you think that was the final answer, and what you think people might get from it, whatever comes to mind.
turns.zh: 我想再回过头来谈谈我们的标志设计，这样能把整个流程串联起来。谈谈最终确定的方案，以及你认为为什么选择这个设计，还有人们可能会从中感受到什么，或者任何你能想到的点。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Yeah, totally. I think the final answer or the final logo, we took it down a lot of different paths trying to see where it was going to land, but ultimately ended up keeping it pretty close to home and really focusing on that asset of the fire. We tried so many different versions of it's microphones with the fire and marshmallows with the fire, et cetera. It was just about sometimes the simplest solution is the correct solution. I don't know, I just feel like in terms of what we were doing for blowing it out and making it really cohesive, we went a lot of directions where there might've been multiple versions of the logo depending on the scale and ultimately ended up in a place where it's much more in line and consistent across the bar.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。我觉得最终的方案或者说最终的标志，我们尝试了很多不同的方向，试图看看它会往哪个方向发展，但最终还是选择了一个比较贴近原意的设计，真正聚焦于火焰这个核心元素。我们尝试了很多版本，比如带有火焰的麦克风、带有火焰的棉花糖等等。有时候最简单的方案往往才是正确的解决方案。我不知道，我只是觉得在我们为品牌推广和保持整体连贯性所做的努力中，我们走了很多方向，可能根据不同尺寸有多个版本的标志，最终却找到了一个在整个品牌中更统一、更连贯的设计。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Maybe what I'll do is we'll share, I don't know if you're comfortable with that, we could just share all the iterations somewhere that we went through.
turns.zh: 是的。或许我可以把我们所有的迭代版本都分享出来，看看你们是否方便接受。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Oh, yeah. I love sharing iterations. It's very fun. Yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，好呀。我很乐意分享迭代版本。这很有趣。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. Sweet. The biggest issue we had with the podcast logo specifically is, originally, I was thinking the mic made sense to differentiate it from the newsletter. At the end of it, it's just like, "Why do we have this freaking mic in there? It just feels strange." That's where we revisited the whole idea and killed the mic and went back to a different version of the fireplace but with marshmallows.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。我们在播客标志设计上遇到的最大问题是，最初我觉得用麦克风能区分它和新闻通讯的不同。但到最后，我们就想：“为什么还要加这个该死的麦克风？感觉很奇怪。” 于是我们重新审视了整个设计思路，去掉了麦克风，换成了带有棉花糖的壁炉图案。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Yeah, I love the marshmallows.
turns.zh: 是的，我喜欢棉花糖。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I love it. That was my wife's... My wife loves the marshmallows also, and it's so versatile. We can use it in so many different ways.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我也喜欢。这是我妻子……我妻子也喜欢棉花糖，而且它用途广泛。我们能用它来做很多不同的设计。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Indeed.
turns.zh: 确实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I guess maybe one last thread there is we explored handwritten typography that you created from scratch, and then there's the block letters. Maybe just thoughts on those two options and benefits and why go one direction versus another?
turns.zh: 我想最后再提一下我们探索的从零开始手写字体，以及块状字体。或许可以谈谈这两个选项的优缺点，以及为什么选择一个方向而非另一个？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: The handwritten one, I really liked because I felt like we could bring the line quality of the illustration into the handwriting, but then the only problem with the handwriting is that if you want to blow that out, if you want to include other handwriting throughout the rest of the brand, finding something that matches that perfectly without creating a custom typeface is a whole thing. I really like being able to combine the two, where we have this broader visual vocabulary that we can pull from, because you're going to have headlines, you're going to have subheads, you're going to have all these other uses for typography moving forward. If you just have one thing to pull from, it's a lot harder to work with. It's just nicer when you have a few elements to play with. It's like having a wardrobe. If you have only one shirt and one pair of pants, there's only so many things that you can do. But if you have all these things that work together and can recombine, then you can blow out a brand system much more easily.
turns.zh: 手写字体那部分我特别喜欢，因为我觉得我们能把插图的线条质感融入到手写字体中。但手写字体唯一的问题是，如果你想把它放大使用，或者想在品牌其他部分也应用手写字体，要找到与之完美匹配的字体却并非易事。这让我很开心能将两者结合起来，因为我们有更丰富的视觉词汇库可以调用——毕竟未来还会有标题、副标题等各种排版需求。如果只能从单一字体中获取灵感，那工作起来就困难得多。有多个元素可供灵活搭配时，效果会好得多。这就像拥有一个衣橱：如果只有一件衬衫和一条裤子，你能发挥的空间就很有限。但如果有多个相互协同、可重新组合的元素，就能更轻松地拓展品牌体系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. That's one of my favorite things about working with you, is you create all these different variations of ways to use it. It doesn't always have to be the handwritten one. It could be the blocky outlining one. It's not like, "This is it, don't change anything about this. This is the only way to use it."
turns.zh: 是啊。这也是我最喜欢与你合作的地方之一，你能创造出各种不同的应用方式。它不必总是手写字体。也可以是块状轮廓字体。不是那种“就只能这样，不能改动”的模式。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Well, part of that is because some brands, if you have a massive company, like hundreds of employees generating hundreds of things, sometimes having too many assets can overcomplicate stuff. Because unless you have a really, really well-written brand book outlining how to do everything that people are adhering to very closely, you can get the assets running rampant throughout all of the stuff and being used incorrectly. But because you're not a massive company and you have creative control over the things that are happening and can help direct that, we can be much more playful with the assets and give you the ability to use things in different ways. It depends on how much you trust all the people that are handling your assets. (00:41:43): I am of the mind that you shouldn't need a 500-page brand book in order to direct how the brand is used moving forward, and that if you do, the brand might be quite complicated, or there might be even just parts of the logo that make it difficult to work with. My goal always when designing a logo is to design a logo that's so easy to use that you don't have to be an extremely skilled designer to design well with it. That's my number one goal, because I know not everybody is going to be at a stage where they have an internal brand team or a designer that's a rock star designer that can work with really complicated assets and make them look good. (00:42:28): I just want the assets to teach you themselves, by just how they exist, how to use it. You, as a person that has any taste whatsoever, and hopefully people that you're hiring for any job at your company have some degree of taste. If you hire an engineer, they have to have taste about how that happens. If you hire a marketing person, they have to have taste about how that happens. They should be able to look at that and intuit most of the way that you should be able to use it without being explicitly told, "Do not do this."
turns.zh: 嗯，部分原因在于有些品牌，比如大型公司，数百名员工创造出数百种资产。有时过多的资产会让事情变得过于复杂。因为除非你有一本精心编写的品牌手册，严格规范所有使用规则，否则资产可能会在各种场合被误用。但由于你们不是大型公司，你对创意有自主控制权，可以引导方向，所以我们能更灵活地处理资产，让你们以不同方式使用它们。这取决于你对处理资产的人有多信任。（00:41:43）：我认为不需要500页的品牌手册来指导品牌后续使用，如果有的话，那品牌可能太复杂了，或者甚至只是标志的某些部分难以处理。我的设计目标始终是设计易于使用的标志，让不需极高设计技能也能出色应用。这是我的首要任务，因为我知道并非所有人都有内部品牌团队或顶级设计师来处理复杂资产并让它们美观。（00:42:28）：我希望资产本身就能教会你如何使用。只要它们存在，你就能通过直观理解如何应用。作为有一定审美眼光的人——希望你公司招聘的任何员工也都有一定审美——如果你雇佣工程师，他们得对技术有审美眼光；如果你雇佣市场人员，他们得对营销有审美眼光。他们应该能看懂这些资产，并能在无需被明确告知“别这么做”的情况下，大致理解如何使用它们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Merge. Product leaders, yes, like you, cringe when they hear the word integration. They're not fun for you to scope, build, launch, or maintain, and integrations probably aren't what led you to product work in the first place. Lucky for you, the folks at Merge are obsessed with integrations. Their single API helps SaaS companies launch over 200 product integrations in weeks, not quarters. Think of Merge like Plaid, but for everything B2B SaaS. Organizations like Ramp, Dorado, and Electric use Merge to access their customer's accounting data to reconcile bill payments, file storage data to create searchable databases and their product, or HRAS data to auto provision and deprovision access for the customer's employees. Yes, if you need AI-ready data for your SaaS product, then Merge is the fastest way to get it. Want to solve your organization's integration dilemma once and for all, book and attend a meeting at merge.dev/lenny and receive a $50 Amazon gift card. That's merge.dev/lenny. (00:44:08): This is a good circle back to something you touched on earlier that I wanted to come back to, which is a lot of companies, in your opinion, put too much weight on the power of brand, and rebranding, and how much a brand can fix their problems. Can you just again share your perspective on just how this might be an issue for people where they almost overemphasize the power of brand? [inaudible 00:44:32]
turns.zh: 本期节目由 Merge 赞助。产品负责人们，特别是像你们这样的人，一听到“集成”这个词就心生畏惧。集成不仅在需求分析、开发、上线和维护过程中令人头疼，而且很可能也不是你们最初投身产品工作的初衷。不过好在 Merge 团队对集成深有研究。他们基于单一 API 帮助 SaaS 公司在数周而非数月内完成 200 余项产品集成。可以把 Merge 想象成 B2B SaaS 领域的 Plaid，适用于所有场景。Ramp、Dorado 和 Electric 等公司利用 Merge 接入客户的会计数据以便核对支付款项，访问存储数据以构建可搜索数据库，或获取 HRAS 数据为客户员工自动授权和注销权限。没错，如果你的 SaaS 产品需要 AI 适用的数据，Merge 是获取这些数据的最快途径。想一劳永逸地解决组织的集成难题？请访问 merge.dev/lenny 预约会议，即可获赠 50 美元亚马逊礼品卡。（00:44:08）：这正好让我回归到之前提到的观点——在你看来，许多公司过度强调品牌的力量和品牌重塑的重要性，认为品牌能解决所有问题。能否再谈谈你对这种现象的看法？即人们过于高估品牌的魔力。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Yeah. Well, there's different companies. There's companies where brand is literally everything, where they're doing something that's not crazy innovative in the first place and the brand is the thing that is the whole company, and that's fine. That's a completely valid way to do stuff. It's like people that can take in information and recommunicate it in a way to another audience or whatever that they hit that audience in a way that the original information couldn't do. Think about all of the people who write books on psychology, and medicine, and all kinds of stuff that write it for a broader popular audience. They're the ones reading the medical papers, they're the ones digesting all of this really huge complicated data, and turning it into something that normal people can read. I think that there are companies that are doing that. They're taking a thing that is not innovative or isn't like they're not the only ones doing it, but they're repackaging it in a way that takes that and makes it so accessible to so many people. (00:45:34): In that case, brand can matter immensely, where the brand really is the thing that shows people that the thing that you're doing has value. But for a lot of people, the brand should be somewhat invisible so that the thing itself becomes the star. If we think about the experiences that we have using products, sometimes there's products where there's a ton of fun and delight built into how you use it, and that can happen through brand through design choices and things like that. Sometimes the delight is the fact that nothing is getting in your way as you're using that product. You just figure out what's your ethos of your company. Is the whole thing about doing a thing well, doing it simply, and making sure that everything gets out of the way of that experience, or is it like we're trying to generate this delightful thing or we're trying to open it up to a new audience or whatever? Depending on whatever that goal is, brand can have a different place in that equation.
turns.zh:
是的。不同的公司情况各异。有些公司把品牌视为一切核心，他们本质上做的事情并非极具创新性，但品牌本身就是整个公司的灵魂，这完全没问题。这是一种完全合理的运营方式。就好比有些人能将信息重新包装，转换为适合特定受众的表达方式。比如那些为大众读者撰写心理学、医学等领域书籍的人。他们深入阅读医学论文，消化海量复杂数据，并将其转化为普通人易懂的知识。我认为有些公司正在这样做。他们接手一个本无创新性的项目，或非唯一在做此事的公司，但通过重新包装，使其触手可及。
（00:45:34）：在这种情况下，品牌至关重要，它向人们传递出产品价值的信号。但对许多公司而言，品牌应当隐形化，让产品本身成为焦点。如果回想我们使用产品的体验，有时产品会通过趣味性和愉悦感提升使用体验，这可能源于品牌设计或其他设计选择。有时愉悦感则在于使用过程中毫无阻碍。关键在于明确公司的核心理念：是专注做好一件事，保持简单，确保一切不阻碍用户体验？还是试图创造惊喜体验、开拓新用户群体等？根据不同目标，品牌在其中所处的地位也各不相同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think some of this unique perspective on the power brand and the need for it in tech companies comes from you're not like a tech person. You work with tech people, you work with tech companies. Do you feel like that has an impact on the way you think and the value that you bring to companies to give them this very outside perspective?
turns.zh: 我认为，你对品牌力量及其在科技公司中的必要性的独特见解，源于你本质上并非技术人员。你与技术人员共事，与科技公司打交道。但你是否觉得这影响了你的思维方式，以及你为公司提供的价值——即从外部视角为其注入新思路？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: I mean, most of the folks that I know that work in brand or traditional graphic design, print design, they don't necessarily have a lot of insight into how building companies works. They're not friends with a ton of startup founders and things like that. I've just had been in this very fun position being like everyone's token creative person in The Bay for a while, and this been for a long time. I remember speaking at a Silicon Valley event that was women in Silicon Valley in 2009 or 2010, something like that. It's interesting to be a person that has never actually, themselves, worked at a tech company but felt so involved and understanding about how all of that works. My partner, the reason why we're in The Bay is because he got hired by Facebook back in 2011. We were olds at the time. Take that with a grain of salt, don't judge me. (00:48:02): Because we were 28, 29 coming over to work at Facebook and everybody there was 23, 24, and so all the people that we ended up meeting in The Bay were more people our age that were moving on to start companies and things like that. We just got to see that perspective so clearly of what it is to branch out on your own, to fundraise, to do all this stuff, to pivot, to do little experimental apps and see where that goes to get acquired as a team versus getting acquired as a technology or whatever. I've been able to see that in a way that I feel like a lot of people that do my job don't get to see. That makes me very sympathetic and towards what it is to want to build a brand as a founder. I understand that you have limited resources and those resources aren't necessarily going to get devoted to doing a $200,000 brand exploration, because when you have $500,000 of money at all for a year to try to get things going, you certainly should not spend half of that money on branding. (00:49:12): That's my opinion, but that's not to say that brand can't be important and can't come in at some level or can't be thought of as a partnership between you and someone else where... There's this whole idea of fractional leadership now, which I feel like hasn't really infiltrated my world as much, but I don't know why it hasn't, because most people don't have internal comms teams, internal brand teams, until the company is very mature. The idea that you could bring someone in who is a real expert in whatever it's that they do, just as you need them, and they just get consultant equity kind of thing, that should be more present because people don't necessarily need to have internal brand teams for the first six months to a year of when they're doing stuff unless they grow really significantly.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我认识的大多数从事品牌或传统平面设计、印刷设计的人，对科技公司的运作机制并没有太多深入了解。他们与创业公司的创始人等圈子交集不多。我曾在湾区担任过一个很有趣的角色——成为所有人的创意顾问，这种状态持续了很久。我记得在2009或2010年参加过硅谷女性活动，那场合很有意思。作为从未真正在科技公司工作过，却对其运作机制了如指掌的人，这种身份挺有趣的。我的合伙人之所以来湾区，是因为2011年他被Facebook录用了。那时我们已经人到中年（大家别太较真，别拿这事儿说笑）。因为我们28、29岁就来Facebook工作，周围的同事都是23、24岁。所以在湾区结识的大多是同龄人，他们后来创办公司之类的。我们得以清晰地看到自主创业、融资、转型、开发小型实验性应用并最终被收购等全过程，而这些与单纯收购技术团队有本质区别。我能以一种大多数同行无法感同身受的方式理解这一切。这让我对创始人想要打造品牌的需求心怀共鸣。我深知他们资源有限，不可能投入20万美元进行品牌探索，因为当你一年只有50万美元启动资金时，肯定不该把一半花在品牌上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines, you have a pretty unique way of pricing your work. For people that may want to explore this with you, share whatever you can about just how you think about pricing and ideally even an order magnitude of pricing so they're like, "Oh, okay. We should actually do this."
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，你在定价方面有独特的方法。对于想探讨此事的人，能否分享一下你的定价思路？理想情况下，能否给出一个定价范围，让他们一目了然：“哦，原来应该这么做。”

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: To go back to the process how it's always about figuring out what people are trying to accomplish, so a lot of my process scales depending on how broad of an exploration that we're doing. The way that I treat it is I treat my branding work not dissimilarly to how I treat commercial lettering, which is atypical. Brand people, what they typically do is because the client has to own the assets outright at the end no matter what, they tend to do is bill everything that the client owns everything as you are moving along. It's all sort of work for hire, but the idea being that it's a buyout of everything that is being made. What that means is that when a branding agency is pricing stuff for you, they're taking the buyout rights and baking it into every round of work so that every round gets more expensive because you are owning all of the work. (00:51:14): What I do is I treat it much more like a commercial lettering project where I say, "You have to own the rights to this eventually, but hey, let's break that out and let's keep the creative process lighter and less expensive so then we have more room to explore. So then if some stakeholder comes in last minute and blows everything else up and we need to start over, you haven't already paid to own everything that we've created, you just pay to own the thing that we create in the end that gets chosen." I really like the idea of keeping the creation process more flexible and to try to scale to what people need versus having a really rigid way of approaching everything. Sometimes people will bring me on really early in the process, where if they have an internal team or if they're working with an external agency or something, they want me there from the get out. (00:52:04): Some people are like, "We have no money and we are going to try to do this as much as we can inside of our business, but then can we hire you at the end to make it look good? If we can get everybody bought in and get it 80% of the way there." Depending on what people's budgets are, I have different ways of working, or just depending on what their needs are. Because my whole thing too is I don't want to step on anybody's toes, because sometimes companies have these really amazing designers that are working in-house, and it sucks as a designer who started at a company and thinks that you might be able to get a chance to work on what is considered the most important asset in terms of the brand and they just farm it out to someone else instead of letting you touch it. To me, that's a recipe for anything that I create to be immediately killed, because someone inside is going to be like, "It's time to shine," and then they're just going to kill all my work. (00:52:56): I'm always like, "How do we collaborate? How do I make it so that I'm an asset to you? Not that I'm trying to step on your toes, not that I'm trying to take over what's the cool juicy work from the people who inside that are really excited to do it." I just want them to feel as bought in as I can be. But yeah, it becomes interesting. I feel like I get told by branding people that I'm too inexpensive because they're like, "Oh, for what you do, it should be 60 or $70,000 at a minimum to do all this kind of stuff." I'm like, I feel like the majority of the projects that I do end up being between 25 and 35, but depending on how you bring me in, it can be less if it's just as a consultant. It's not out of the realm of possibilities to hire a proper crazy expert at stuff. It's not like you're thinking about sinking half a million dollars into the brand. That's a very different experience.
turns.zh:
回到这个过程——关键在于要先弄清楚客户的需求是什么。因此，我的创作流程会根据项目的探索范围而有所调整。我的处理方式与商业字体设计类似，但又有所不同。传统品牌设计公司通常会要求客户在项目结束时完全拥有所有资产，因此他们会把所有权授予客户，逐步收取费用。这其实是一种买断制，但这意味着客户必须在项目结束时购买所有创作成果。（00:51:14）而我的做法是，把创作过程看作商业字体项目。我会说：“最终你们肯定会拥有这些资产，但先把权利分开，让创作过程更灵活、成本更低。这样即便最后有利益相关方临时介入导致项目重头开始，你们也不必为已完成的部分买单，只需为最终选定的成果付费。”我非常推崇保持创作灵活性的理念，根据客户需求调整策略，而非一刀切的模式。有时客户很早就邀请我参与项目——比如内部团队或外部代理机构——希望我从一开始就参与其中。（00:52:04）有些客户会说：“我们预算有限，想先内部完成大部分工作，等最后再请你润色。”这取决于他们的预算和需求。我会根据实际情况调整工作方式，因为我不想踩到别人的地盘。有些公司内部有优秀的设计师，但他们把最重要的品牌资产外包出去，让你只能旁观，这无疑会扼杀你的创作热情。（00:52:56）我总是在想：“如何合作？如何让你们觉得我有价值？我不是想抢风头，也不是想夺走内部团队热衷的酷炫项目。”我只想让他们充分认可我的价值。这确实很有挑战性。我常被品牌设计师批评收费过低，他们说：“你的服务费至少该6万到7万美元。”但我的大部分项目收费在25到35美元之间。当然，如果你只是以顾问身份参与，费用会更低。花几十万美元打造品牌也不是不可行，但绝不是大多数项目的常态。
截然不同的体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Thank you for sharing that. Before we get into other stuff that you do, because like you said at the top, there are many other things you do outside of this specific time of work, is there anything else you think might be helpful or important for people to know about working with you on a logo refresh or just thinking about logos and this whole space we talked about?
turns.zh: 太棒了。感谢你分享这些内容。在我们深入探讨你其他工作之前——正如你开头所说，除了当前的工作时段，你在其他领域也有诸多作为——你觉得还有哪些方面对与你合作进行标志更新，或者对思考标志设计及相关领域可能有所帮助或重要呢？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: The best thing is just seeing what's there and really being able to understand what's not working about it and what your goals are. Like I said with that reverse justification of intuition, I think if you know that the logo is not quite where you want it to be, just spend a couple days asking yourself why. "What is the thing about this that bothers me?" Don't get specific. Don't be like, "The way the R is," or whatever. Maybe that's the thing that we talk about down the line, but always think big picture before you think minutiae, because sometimes people think that... They'll throw a bunch of minutiae stuff at me, but it's because they haven't really stopped to think about what is the overall thing that's bothering them. (00:54:59): You just never get there if you're always trying to address detail before you address the big picture stuff. You have to just always start super top level, and really ask yourself very broad questions about why you think it's not working, and then go tighter, and tighter, and tighter, and be like... It really could be like, "This C has always bothered me," and then we can get real specific about that when I'm doing the refresh. But I think I also need to understand the overall reason why we're doing this, not just the little bugaboo that bothers you specifically but might not bother anybody else.
turns.zh: 最重要的是先观察现有情况，然后真正理解其存在的问题和你的设计目标。正如我之前提到的反向直觉验证法，如果你意识到标志设计未达预期，只需花几天时间自问：“这个设计哪里让我感到不满？”别过于纠结细节，比如“R字母的处理方式”之类的。这些细节或许我们之后再探讨，但在深入之前先把握大局至关重要。（00:54:59）：如果你总是在处理细节之前先纠缠于具体问题，就永远无法触及核心。必须从最高层面入手，先广泛思考设计不达标的原因，再逐步深入，最终才能具体探讨某个细节。例如，“这个C字母一直让我不满意”，等我实际进行更新时再深入探讨。但我认为更重要的是理解整体设计初衷，而非仅关注某个特定困扰你的细节，那些细节或许对其他人毫无意义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. When I was thinking about this, it feels like my whole feeling was this could be better. That's all it was for me initially, is just like I feel like it could be a lot better. I imagine that's enough for some people, just like, "I think this could be better," and then here's things [inaudible 00:55:50].
turns.zh: 是的。我最初思考这个问题时，最大的感受就是它本可以更出色。这就是我最初的想法——觉得它本可以做得更好。想必对某些人来说，这就足够了，只要觉得“可以做得更好”即可，然后再具体探讨（00:55:50）。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Yeah. That's definitely enough for some people, because I think sometimes... I think you, specifically, had a very clear vibe going on with all of your brand stuff. Some people, it's totally like a mishmash grab bag of random trends and there's no real voice that's coming through. But I feel like you've been doing this for a while, and when you see everything together, there's definitely a very clear vision and vibe that you get from everything. I always tell people that having terrible vision can be your best asset when it comes to logo and brand, because it allows you... (00:56:30): Just take your glasses off if you have terrible vision, and look at it, and get the feeling when you can't see the detail. You have to be looking at it with blurred eyes. What is the overall look of this thing? Just trying to get as broad and noodly as you can with it instead of it being about those really specific one by one stuff. I think when you blur your eyes on your brand, there was a really clear cohesiveness to it already. It was just about massaging it into a more consistent professional-looking place.
turns.zh: 是的。对某些人来说，这确实足够了。因为我觉得有时候……比如你，显然对自己的品牌设计有清晰的构想。而有些人则是一堆杂乱无章的流行趋势拼凑，没有任何统一的风格。但我觉得你从事这行已经有一段时间了，当你审视整体作品时，能明显感受到其背后统一的理念和风格。我总是告诉人们，在标志和品牌设计中，糟糕的视觉感知反而可能是最大的优势，因为它能让你……（00:56:30）：如果你视力不好，可以摘下眼镜，直观观察，感受看不清细节时的整体效果。必须以模糊的视角审视品牌设计，寻找其背后统一的脉络。即便你的品牌设计已然存在明显的连贯性，但还需要将其打磨得更专业、更一致。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, I can't look at the old logo anymore now that I've gotten this thing coming together, so I'm really excited for this to come out. Just a couple closing questions. One is you have a lot of other stuff going on that is not just typography and logo refreshes. You have children's books, you do lettering for classics, you have a store in Oakland. Talk about all these other things you got going on in case it might interest people.
turns.zh: 嗯，现在我已经把这件事处理得差不多了，所以我再也看不下去那个旧标志了。真期待它最终能正式发布。最后再问几个问题吧。首先，你做的远不止是字体设计和标志更新。你还写儿童书籍，为经典作品创作字体设计，在奥克兰开了一家店。能不能跟我们讲讲你其他的业务？说不定能吸引一些感兴趣的人呢。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Sure. Yeah, of course. I'm based here in The Bay, as we've talked about, and I have a studio in Downtown Oakland. My studio is like Barbie's creative Dream house, where the top floor is my office, that's where I'm right now, and then the bottom floor on one side is a workshop. I do a lot of printmaking. I went to college at a school that was very focused on interdisciplinary work, and I feel like I bring a lot of manual analog processes into my work a lot. I find it really important to make physical things as a part of my creative process, so I do a lot of printmaking. On the other side downstairs is a brick and mortar store. I've always wanted to have a brick and mortar store because, as an artist, I think having people have a physical connection to your work can be really important. (00:58:20): I think one of the reasons why people hire me to do things for them is because one of the gifts of working with someone that is a real nerd professional about whatever it is that they do is that they bring you along the journey and give you the language to talk about the thing through their eyes and through their experience. To me, the funnest thing for me is actually telling clients and teaching them about all the things that we are doing along the way so then they go out into the world as a newly-minted type nerd and can communicate all of these things to other people. That connection is just really important. The connection to the work, the story behind it, I feel like that's one of the ways that we create lasting work, is understanding that the work exists because there's a story behind it. Things, if they're just created because of the aesthetics or they're just created quickly or whatever, it's really easy to discard them because there's not a story behind it. (00:59:22): But if you think about all the objects in your life that have followed you throughout your life, what's a thing that you've had since you were in fifth grade or whatever that is still magically in your possession in your house? You have that because the story of that thing is so important to you. I think that the work that we create, the design that we create, can have that. It can be imbued with so much story and meaning, that when we think about moving on from it, we're like, "Ugh, but this." I think that's one of the ways to build a lasting brand, is to just make sure that the story of creating it feels so real, and visceral, and important. The store is a way for people to have a physical connection to other work that I create, like the prints and things like that. (01:00:07): With the kids' book stuff, that's also about creating lasting stuff. I like creating physical things in the world. I like repackaging things that I've learned in therapy in a way that kids will appreciate and enjoy. I'm just always thinking about what's a way that I can say a thing that has been said before but hasn't been said in this way. If I can turn that into a physical object that people can have and appreciate, all the better. But yeah, I don't know. While, professionally, what I do is considered very niche, I feel like all the things that I do are quite diverse, because they tickle different parts of my brain. I have to use my hands in different ways and my mind in different ways. It's how I've been able to generally avoid feeling burnt out as a creative, is just being able to move on between different kinds of work and just feel excited about different things at different times.
turns.zh:
好的。是的，当然可以。我现在住在旧金山湾区，正如我们之前聊过的，我在奥克兰市中心还有一间工作室。我的工作室就像芭比的创意梦想屋，顶层是我的办公室，我现在就在这里，而底层一侧是工作间，我经常在那里进行版画创作。我上大学的学校非常注重跨学科学习，我觉得自己在创作中融入了许多手工模拟流程。我认为亲手制作实体作品是创意过程中至关重要的一环，所以我特别热爱版画制作。另一侧的底层是实体商店。我一直想开一家实体店，因为作为艺术家，我觉得让人们能亲身接触你的作品非常重要。  

（00:58:20）我认为人们雇我做事的原因之一，是因为与真正精通某一领域的专业人士合作，能带你走入他们的创作之旅，让你用他们的视角和经验来理解事物。对我来说，最有趣的事情就是向客户讲解并教会他们我们在创作过程中的种种细节，这样他们就能带着新学到的知识走入社会，向他人传递这些信息。这种联系至关重要。作品背后的故事和创意逻辑，是我们打造经久不衰作品的关键所在。若作品只是为了美观而创作，或者是草草拼凑而成，很容易被淘汰，因为缺乏内在意义。  

（00:59:22）但想想你生活中那些伴随多年的物品，比如五年级就拥有的某样东西，至今仍安静地摆在家里。这是因为它承载着你的珍贵记忆。我相信我们创作的作品和设计作品也能注入同样的情感和意义。当我们要舍弃它们时，总会心痛不已。这就是打造持久品牌的秘诀——确保创作故事真实、深刻且重要。实体店能让人们亲手触摸我的其他作品，比如版画之类的。  

（01:00:07）儿童书籍系列同样秉持着这种理念。我喜欢在现实世界中创造实体物品，用孩子们能理解的方式重新包装我在心理治疗中领悟的道理。我总在思考如何用新的方式讲述老掉牙的故事。如果能把这些转化为人们能触摸和欣赏的实物，那就再好不过了。虽然从专业角度看，我所从事的领域被视为小众，但我觉得自己的多元化实践能激活大脑不同区域，让我在不同类型的创作中保持热情，避免职业倦怠。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For folks that want to maybe check out the store, how do they find it? It's called Jessica and Friends, is that right?
turns.zh: 想去店里看看的朋友，该怎么找到它呢？店名叫Jessica and Friends，对吧？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Yes. It's called Jessica Hische and Friends.
turns.zh: 对。店名是Jessica Hische and Friends。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jessica Hische and Friends.
turns.zh: Jessica Hische and Friends。

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: You can just Google JH&F.
turns.zh: 你可以在谷歌上搜JH&F。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Google Maps, yeah. [inaudible 01:01:17]
turns.zh: 谷歌地图啊，对。[语音不清 01:01:17]

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Yeah. I put JH&F on as a part of the Google Maps name so I don't have to spell my name to strangers, because I have a weird German spelling last name. I also have a second store called Drawling, which is drawing with an L thrown in there. That one is an all-ages art supply store that's sort of a kids' art supply store. That one grew out of JH&F as well. Those two stores exist. With my books, if you just look up my last name on any of your favorite booksellers, you'll find me.
turns.zh: 对。我把JH&F作为谷歌地图名称的一部分，这样就不用给陌生人拼写我的名字了，因为我的姓氏拼写比较奇特，带有L的德国拼法。另外我还有一家叫Drawling的店，名字是Drawling，里面加了个L。这是一家面向所有年龄段的艺术用品店，算是一家儿童艺术用品店。它也是从JH&F发展出来的。这两家店都存在。至于我的书，如果你在喜欢的书店上搜索我的姓氏，都能找到我的作品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Last question. I'm just going to throw this out there in case something interesting comes up. We have a segment on this podcast called AI Corner, where I like to see how people have found ways to use AI in their work, in their life to be more productive, do cool things. Is there some way that you've found a way to use AI in the work that you do that makes you do more interesting stuff?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。我就随便问问，看看有没有什么有趣的回答。我们播客有个叫AI Corner的环节，我想了解大家如何在工作和生活中利用AI提高效率、做些酷事。你的工作中有没有用到AI，从而做出了更有趣的东西？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: A little bit. I am in this really interesting position in terms of AI where my partner works at Meta on GenAI stuff. He's a director on the GenAI team at Meta and is very bought into AI as a whole thing. I am a little [inaudible 01:02:28] about its impact on a lot of the things that we do. I think, overall, it will become a tool and be very useful, especially in a lot of different fields. But I think this timeframe in which it's more novelty is going to have not the best impact on things like illustration, but eventually, we'll all come out of it and it'll be fine. In terms of how I've been able to integrate it into my process, I did some work for Salesforce last year where the theme for Dreamforce was going to be very AI-driven. I felt like I needed to explore AI as a part of the generative process for creating that art. (01:03:08): I did have fun creating custom lettering and then trying to run it through stable diffusion to get stable diffusion to generate instances of my lettering in different styles. We were making these clouds. We ultimately didn't end up using it, but it was still really neat to see. I could see the validity of that in the creative iterative process. I think the biggest thing for me is that I find that the sloggy, slow dregs of work is very fulfilling to me, that a lot of the evangelists of AI are like, "Oh, imagine if you could spend all of your time high level thinking, and coming up with the concepts, and guiding the vision, and whatever, and then just get AI to do everything else that you don't care about." For me, that just sounds like not the most holistic approach to how I work, because the reason why I do all the things that I do and why my process is the way that it is because while I love thinking and I love coming up with conceptual stuff, I find it to be very cerebrally taxing. (01:04:17): I need a break from that by doing the more low-key production end of stuff. That's my favorite part of the process, is we know what we're doing, and now it's just about going in. When it comes to judging logos, for instance, the days that I spend knowing exactly what I'm going to do and all it is me just moving little Bezier handles around and getting it feeling right and whatever, those are pure therapeutic zen for me. I think I will always have that as a part of my work and will probably not have AI be outputting that part. But I have been able to have it be helpful in the iterative process a little bit, both through generating sketches with that project and then also through a lot of stuff with writing with my kids' books and things like that, is coming up with lists of words and concepts that are adjacent to each other, whatever. (01:05:17): I have found that Claude and ChatGPT are very good for things like that. I'm working on another kids' book now, and I'm trying to think of the directions that it can take. One of them is sort of illustrating different feelings and things like that. I could sit there and brainstorm what are the different emotions or whatever, or I can just ask Claude like, "List 50 emotions," and then I can cherry-pick the ones that come up that feel right. I do find it's really good for that early brainstorming stuff, and that's been really nice.
turns.zh:
是的，我在人工智能领域处于一个非常有趣的位置。我的搭档在Meta公司负责GenAI相关项目，他对人工智能整体非常热衷。我对它对我们工作的影响持谨慎态度。我认为，总体而言，它会成为一种工具，非常有用，尤其是在许多不同领域。但目前，它更多地被视为一种新奇事物，这对插画等领域的影响并不理想。不过最终我们都会走出这个阶段，一切都会好起来的。  

关于我如何将其融入创作流程，去年我为Salesforce做了一个项目，当时Dreamforce大会的主题将围绕人工智能展开。我觉得有必要探索人工智能在生成艺术过程中的作用。我们制作了一些云形图案，最终虽然没有用上，但看到效果还是很棒的。我能在创意迭代过程中看到其价值。对我来说，最重要的是，我觉得那些缓慢而繁琐的工作环节其实很有意义。很多人工智能的宣传者会说：“想象一下，如果你能把所有时间都花在高层次的思考上，构思概念、指导方向等等，然后让AI处理所有你不关心的部分。”但对我来说，这听起来并不是最全面的工作方式，因为我之所以做现在所做的一切，之所以形成这样的工作流程，是因为我热爱思考和构思创意，但这对我来说太耗费脑力了。  

（01:04:17）我需要通过处理更基础的制作工作来放松大脑。这是我在创作过程中最喜欢的部分——我们清楚接下来要做什么，现在只需要开始行动。比如在评判标志设计时，那些我确切知道要做什么的日子——只需调整贝塞尔曲线手柄，让设计感觉自然等等，对我来说就是纯粹的放松疗法。我想这部分工作我会一直坚持下去，可能不会让AI来完成。但在迭代过程中，人工智能确实能提供一些帮助，无论是通过生成草图，还是在儿童书籍创作中列出相邻词汇和概念等，都很有用。  

（01:05:17）我发现Claude和ChatGPT在这些方面非常有用。我现在正在创作另一本儿童书籍，正在思考可能的创作方向之一。其中一个方向是描绘不同情感等。我可以坐下来头脑风暴各种情感，但也可以直接问Claude：“列出50种情感”，然后挑选合适的词汇。这对早期构思阶段真的很有帮助，体验很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else that you want to share or leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 在进入令人兴奋的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想和听众分享或留给他们的吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
turns.en: Yes. Well, I do have a new kid's book coming out in October.
turns.zh: 是的。嗯，我确实有一本新儿童书籍将于10月出版。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, [inaudible 01:06:02].

turns.speaker: Jessica Hische
